name: Mariya Nurislamova
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED: ycombinator.com/companies/scentbird names "Mariya Nurislamova" as Founder with the one-liner "Scentbird is a luxury fragrance subscription service." (Founded 2013, batch Summer 2015), and Scentbird is entry 58 of the 91-company Y Combinator Top Companies list fetched directly from https://yc-oss.github.io/api/companies/top.json (verified by downloading the JSON and indexing it, not by trusting the roster). SERIAL-FOUNDER CHECK -- SHE IS ONE, AND SCENTBIRD IS STILL THE HIT: YC's own conference bio describes her as "a serial entrepreneur having co-founded an IT-outsourcing company and a fashion startup in the past". Those two are Neuvey (co-founder and COO, Sep 2011 - Nov 2013) and Missionelle (founder and CEO, Nov 2012 - Jul 2013), both named in her scraped work history at aeroleads.com/p/mariyanurislamova and both listed independently at nocap.blog/founder/mariya-nurislamova/ alongside Beta Week, The Iris Organization and Xtreme Mobile. Neither produced any revenue figure in any source; both were sub-two-year ventures that closed while she was still working as a speed-reading coach and masseuse (woman.forumdaily.com profile), and the 2012 and 2013 rev10 bars are $6.6M-$6.8M nominal. No earlier venture came remotely near the bar, so the first venture to cross is Scentbird. BOUNDED rev10 2016-2018, both ends sourced. LOWER END: TechCrunch, 30 March 2016, reports Scentbird at a "$6 million run rate" -- against the 2016 rev10 bar of $7,454,953 that is below threshold, so the crossing cannot predate 2016. FLAG: this is a MARGIN UNDER 20% (6.0/7.455 = 19.5% below the bar) and it is an annualised run rate taken in March of a fast-growing year, not a full-year figure, so the lower end is the weakest part of this row; the founding year (2013, per YC's company page; TechCrunch says the company came out of the Entrepreneurs Roundtable Accelerator in 2014 and forumdaily says work began August 2013) would give a safer but four-year-looser lower bound of 2013. UPPER END: Beauty Independent (May 2018) reports over 250,000 subscribers at $14.95/month with 95% of sales from subscriptions, an annualised $44.9M against the 2018 bar of $7,799,735 -- 5.8x the bar, no ambiguity. The same article's "subscription sales jumped 110% year-over-year" implies roughly $21M in 2017, which would put the crossing at 2016 or 2017, but that is a derived level from a stated growth rate rather than a sourced 2017 revenue figure, so the upper end is left at 2018 rather than narrowed. Span 2016-2018 is two years, well inside the ten-year limit; midpoint 2017. a1: UNKNOWN. Three sources with biographical detail (equilar ExecAtlas, woman.forumdaily.com's long Russian-emigre profile, nocap.blog) give no birth year or age. a2: UNKNOWN, and this was chased hard. Her completed credential is a BBA from Baruch College (Zicklin School of Business), CUNY; forumdaily states she finished it in two years and that her earlier Perm Polytechnic applied-mathematics course was LEFT INCOMPLETE (Equilar's listing of two Perm "B.S." degrees is contradicted by her own account, so it is not used). No fetchable source gives the Baruch graduation year: equilar, aeroleads, theorg, cew.org, forumdaily and nocap.blog all list the degree without a year; contactout and crunchbase 403 to both WebFetch and curl with a browser User-Agent; a Baruch-domain alumni search returned nothing naming her. A search-engine synthesis offered "January 2011" but no fetchable page states it, so it is not recorded. a3: JUDGMENT CALL, LOW CONFIDENCE. Her employer-paid roles (Executive Assistant at Xtreme Mobile 2008-2009; New York Regional Director at The Iris Organization Apr 2010 - Dec 2011) are not in the consumer/beauty/subscription-commerce domain that produced the hit, and neither is Neuvey (IT outsourcing). The first role of any kind in the hit's domain is Missionelle, the fashion startup she founded in November 2012, so a3 = 2012 -- the same "first job actually in the craft, not just any job" reasoning used at p33 Morrison and p05 Bong. a4: 2011, Neuvey (Sep 2011), her earliest venture of any kind, not Scentbird -- the dataset's first-thing-founded convention (p26 Roddick's B&B). Confidence medium: the dates come from a LinkedIn-derived aggregator, corroborated in company list but not in dates by nocap.blog. a6: 2019, when she stated an annual turnover of $60M and "more than $5 million per month" to forumdaily -- a later, larger-scale event than the a5 crossing. Confidence low; it is a founder's own unaudited claim in an interview. NOT USED: getlatka.com/companies/scentbird.com gives a 2024 revenue of $43.9M but asserts Scentbird is "bootstrapped ... without raising any venture capital or outside funding", which is flatly false (a $2.8M round in 2016 and an $18.6M Series A in May 2018 are both press-reported), so the whole page is treated as unreliable and none of its figures are used.

name: Jim Ratcliffe
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED: Sunday Times Rich List 2025, rank 7 -- "Sir Jim Ratcliffe | 17.046 | Industry (Ineos)" -- fetched from en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunday_Times_Rich_List_2025, which reproduces the ranked table naming him; corroborated by his own Wikipedia article, which records the Sunday Times Rich List 2018 naming him Britain's wealthiest individual at GBP 21.05bn. The roster's note that thetimes.com returns a 1.3KB shell naming nobody was not re-tested; the Wikipedia reproduction of the ranked table names the person and the rank, which is the standard the brief asks for. SERIAL-FOUNDER CALL -- THE HIT ENTITY IS INSPEC, NOT INEOS. THIS IS THE MAIN JUDGMENT ON THIS ROW AND IT MOVES THE ANCHOR SIX YEARS EARLIER. The roster frames Ineos (1998) as the venture and Ratcliffe's earlier years as "a long apprenticeship as an employee engineer and then a private-equity operator". That framing does not survive checking. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ineos states in its own history section that Ineos "traces its roots to Inspec, established in 1992 by Jim Ratcliffe and John Hollowood"; businesschief.eu and business-sale.com both use co-founding language for the same event (Ratcliffe, then a director at Advent International, partnered with Dr John Hollowood to buy a chemicals division out of BP for about $50M in a management buy-IN, with Hollowood as chairman and Ratcliffe as chief executive). Inspec Group plc was a newly formed company that acquired assets -- structurally the identical move to Ineos in 1998, which was also a new company formed to buy an existing plant (the Antwerp site, for GBP 84M). Bought is not inherited, so frame.md's going-concern bar does not fire: he did not take over a family firm, he formed the acquiring vehicle. Under the study's rule that the hit is the FIRST venture to cross, Inspec displaces Ineos. The counter-case is recorded honestly: at the moment of the 1992 deal he was on Advent's payroll and Advent backed it, so it can be read as a PE portfolio-company CEO appointment rather than his own venture. Two independent sources use founding language and none describes him as merely hired, so the founding reading is taken. Nothing earlier qualifies -- BP, the unnamed pharmaceutical company, Esso, Courtaulds and Advent are all employers, not ventures -- so 1992 Inspec is also a4. BOUNDED rev10 1992-1994, both ends sourced, QUALITATIVE SCALE CLAIM DOING THE DATING WORK (flagged as the brief requires). LOWER END: the founding-year rule -- Inspec did not exist before the 1992 buy-in and cannot have earned before it existed. UPPER END: businesschief.eu records that "1994: Inspec floated on London Stock Exchange valued at $125 million". The 1994 rev10 bar is $4,603,299 nominal; a specialty-chemicals manufacturer carrying a $125M public-market valuation is 27x the bar in valuation terms and cannot plausibly be under $4.6M of sales, and the business it was built on was itself bought from BP for about $50M in 1992 -- 11x the 1992 bar of $4,357,914 in purchase price alone. frame.md explicitly permits a qualitative scale claim to establish that a crossing occurred, leaving only the year to be bounded, and that is exactly what is happening here: NO STATED REVENUE FIGURE FOR INSPEC IN ANY YEAR WAS FOUND despite targeted searching (Laporte plc's Wikipedia page gives only the ~$1bn 1998 takeover price; the only Inspec-specific earnings number found anywhere is that the acquisition contributed GBP 18.1M to Laporte's 1998 pre-tax profits in a four-month stub period, itself far above that year's GBP-converted bar but too late to narrow this bound). The true crossing is most likely 1992 itself, since the entity began life owning an operating BP division rather than as a startup with no sales, so the midpoint of 1993 is if anything late. Span is two years. NO CURRENCY CONVERSION APPLIED: both load-bearing figures ($50M purchase price, $125M flotation valuation) are already quoted in US dollars by the source, so they compare directly against the nominal USD bars. a1: born 18 October 1952, Failsworth, Lancashire (Wikipedia). a2: 1980, MBA in finance from London Business School, studied 1978-1980 and funded by his then employer Esso -- this is the last credential completed, later than his 2:1 in chemical engineering from the University of Birmingham in 1974 (both from Wikipedia, LBS corroborated by businesschief.eu). a3: 1974, medium confidence and a judgment call. On graduating from Birmingham in 1974 he joined BP as a chemical engineer -- squarely the domain that produced the hit -- but was dismissed after three days because eczema made him unsuitable for work with toxic chemicals. He then worked as a trainee accountant at a pharmaceutical company and joined Esso, and spent over a decade at Courtaulds, a chemicals and fabrics producer, into his mid-thirties. No source gives a year for the Esso or Courtaulds start, so the only datable entry into the chemical industry is the 1974 BP hiring; its three-day duration is why confidence is medium rather than high. a6: 2005, the $9bn purchase of BP's Innovene, which per en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ineos "roughly quadrupled Ineos's turnover, which was previously around $8 billion" -- a later, far larger-scale event than the a5 crossing, and the point at which the Ineos rollup became a top-tier global petrochemicals business.

name: Lakshmi Mittal
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED: Sunday Times Rich List 2025, rank 8 -- "Lakshmi Mittal and family | 15.444 | Steel" -- fetched from en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunday_Times_Rich_List_2025, which reproduces the ranked table naming him. Corroborated in depth by his own Wikipedia article, which tabulates his Rich List placings across years (1st in 2006 at GBP 14.88bn, 1st in 2008 at GBP 27.70bn, 7th in 2015 and 2024). INHERITED-FIRM CHECK, THE ONE THE ASSIGNMENT FLAGS: his father Mohanlal Mittal ran the family steel business Nippon Denro Ispat, which Lakshmi joined as a TRAINEE in 1970 after graduating. That going concern is barred as a hit entity by frame.md and is not used. His own venture is PT Ispat Indo, established 1976 in Sidoarjo, East Java, Indonesia -- described by Wikipedia as "his inaugural independent steel factory", founded when Indian government curbs on domestic steel production pushed him abroad at age 26. He built it greenfield rather than taking it over. The Indian family assets stayed with his brothers Pramod and Vinod at the 1994 split, which confirms the separation of the two lines. SERIAL-FOUNDER CHECK: no earlier venture found. Between his 1970 entry into his father's firm and the 1976 Indonesian venture he was an employee of the family business; Ispat Indo is the first thing he founded and also the first to cross. rev10 1978, QUALITATIVE SCALE CLAIM DOING THE DATING WORK -- FLAGGED AS THE BRIEF REQUIRES, AND THIS IS THE WEAKEST POINT OF THE ROW. No source gives a revenue figure for PT Ispat Indo in any year. What is sourced is (a) the plant "opened in Sidoarjo, East Java, Indonesia in 1978 and made money right away" (globalindian.com), and (b) that it "started off as a 60,000T per annum greenfield rolling facility for wire rods" before expanding to around 800,000T of melting/casting/rolling over later decades. The 1978 rev10 bar is $2,025,203 nominal. Wire rod sold for roughly $300/tonne in 1978, so nameplate 60,000 tonnes is on the order of $18M -- roughly 9x the bar -- and the plant would clear the bar at about 11% of nameplate utilisation in its opening year. A first-year crossing is therefore safe by a very wide margin even on a heavily discounted ramp, which is why this is recorded as the exact year 1978 rather than a bounded range: the entity did not exist as a producer before 1978 (so nothing earlier is possible) and it cleared the bar in its first operating year. Confidence is medium, not high, because the crossing rests on capacity plus a stated price level rather than on a published sales figure, and because the plant's 1976 establishment date differs from its 1978 opening date across sources. NO CURRENCY CONVERSION NEEDED: steel wire rod is priced and traded in US dollars and the capacity-derived figure is already in USD; no rupiah or rupee account was used. a1: born 15 June 1950, Sadulpur, Rajasthan (Wikipedia). a2: 1970, B.Com with first-class honours from St. Xavier's College, University of Calcutta (globalindian.com; Wikipedia confirms the college and degree but gives no year, so confidence is medium rather than high). a3: 1970, joined his father's Nippon Denro Ispat as a trainee immediately on graduating -- the same year as a2, and squarely in the steel domain that produced the hit. He had already been working evening shifts at the steel mill from age 19 while studying, so an argument exists for 1969, but 1970 is the first dated full-time role and is what is recorded. a4: 1976, the establishment of PT Ispat Indo, not the 1978 plant opening -- a4 is the founding of the venture, a5 the crossing. a6: 2006-07, the hostile takeover of Arcelor creating ArcelorMittal, the world's largest steel producer -- a later, vastly larger-scale event than the a5 crossing; recorded as 2006, the year the bid succeeded (Wikipedia).

name: Carver Mead
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED: computerhistory.org/profile/carver-mead/ names him as a 2002 Computer History Museum Fellow with the citation "for his contributions in pioneering the automation, methodology and teaching of integrated circuit design" -- an official award page naming the person, fetched directly. SERIAL-FOUNDER CALL, AND IT IS THE HARD PART OF THIS ROW. Wikipedia states Mead "has been involved in the founding of at least 20 companies" and lists eight of the significant ones. By founding date the candidates are Lexitron (word processing), Silicon Compilers Inc. 1981, Actel 1985, Synaptics 1986, Sonix/Sonic Innovations 1991, Silerity (sold to Viewlogic 1995), Foveon c.1999 and Impinj (2000s). LEXITRON CONSIDERED AND REJECTED AS THE HIT ENTITY, WITH THE REASON RECORDED: Lexitron dates from 1969 (the Computer History Archives video Wikipedia cites is titled "Lexitron Word Processing Computer Origin & History 1969-1984") and was acquired by Raytheon in 1977-78, so if it counted it would move this row's a4 and a5 back by more than a decade. It does not count, for two independent reasons. (1) Mead's founder role is asserted in exactly one place -- a bare bullet in Wikipedia's company list, sourced to a Vimeo video -- and three separate searches pairing "Carver Mead" with Lexitron found no other source connecting him to the company, no year for his involvement, and no description of what "involved in the founding" meant. (2) Even granting the role, Lexitron's crossing is undatable: no revenue or sales figure for Lexitron in any year surfaced in any source, and the Raytheon purchase price is not published either, so neither a rev10 date, a bound, nor an acq50 fallback can be built. Recording Lexitron would require inventing both the year and the scale. It is therefore excluded from consideration and Silicon Compilers Inc. is used, with this caveat flagged for re-checking. CONTESTED FOUNDER STATUS AT SCI, ALSO FLAGGED: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carver_Mead states that "Mead, Johannsen, Edmund K. Cheng and others formed Silicon Compilers Inc. (SCI) in 1981", citing David Lammers in IEEE Spectrum and the Computer History Museum's oral history of Edmund Cheng. semiengineering.com's entity page instead lists SCI's founders as David Johannsen, Edmund K. Cheng, L. John Doerr III and Peter Rip, omitting Mead. Wikipedia's version rests on two named primary-ish sources including a CHM oral history and is preferred, but the conflict is real and is recorded rather than smoothed over. SCI grew directly out of Mead's own Caltech work: he and his PhD student David L. Johannsen built the first silicon compiler (Johannsen's "Bristle Blocks", 1979). BOUNDED rev10 1981-1989, both ends sourced, span 8 years, midpoint 1985. LOWER END: the founding-year rule -- SCI was formed in 1981 and cannot have earned before it existed. UPPER END: techmonitor.ai reports that Silicon Compiler Systems "was doing $45m in 1989" with an installed base of over 1,700 chip design seats and close to 400 employees, when Mentor Graphics agreed to buy it for about $110M in 6.3M new shares. The 1989 rev10 bar is $3,851,613 nominal, so $45M is 11.7x the bar -- no margin problem at all. CAVEAT ON THE UPPER END: Silicon Compiler Systems was created in 1987 from the merger of Silicon Design Labs with Silicon Compilers Inc. (same source), so the $45M is the merged company's, not SCI's alone; even attributing only half of it to the SCI side leaves roughly $22M, still 5.8x the bar, so the conclusion is unaffected by the attribution. NOT NARROWED: targeted searching for an SCI revenue figure for 1984, 1985 or 1986 found none; the company was private and its best-known mid-1980s milestone (designing one of the key chips for DEC's MicroVAX, and the 1986 VTC process deal for Genesil users) carries no dollar figure. The 1990 Mentor acquisition at $110M would clear the acq50 bar easily, but the fallback is BARRED here because an earlier crossing is known to have occurred (the 1989 revenue figure itself proves it), exactly as frame.md requires. a1: born 1 May 1934, Bakersfield, California (Wikipedia; CHM profile confirms 1934 and Bakersfield). a2: 1960, PhD in Electrical Engineering from Caltech, after a BS in 1956 and an MS in 1957 -- 1960 is given by Wikipedia (citing Caltech's own CNS faculty page and the Caltech Archives oral history), by Caltech's own carvermead.caltech.edu/biography ("BS ('56), MS ('57) and PhD ('60)") and by lemelson.mit.edu. DISCREPANCY NOTED: the Computer History Museum's own Fellow profile says the PhD was 1959; it is outvoted 3-1 by Caltech's own pages and is not used. a3: 1960, LOW CONFIDENCE AND THE WEAKEST ANCHOR ON THIS ROW. Mead never left Caltech -- he was a teaching assistant as an undergraduate, taught through graduate school, and retired in 1999 after 40-plus years on the faculty -- and no fetchable source gives the year he converted from student/TA to faculty. Two attempts (caltech.edu's "The Life of a Caltech Lifer" feature and Caltech's own carvermead.caltech.edu biography) both describe the continuous career without dating the appointment. 1960 is recorded as the year his independent work in the hit's domain begins: it is both the PhD year and the year Wikipedia records him as "the first person to describe and demonstrate a three-terminal solid-state device based on the operating principles of electron tunneling and hot-electron transport". a4: 1981, Silicon Compilers Inc. See the Lexitron discussion above -- if Mead's Lexitron founding role were ever properly sourced with a year, a4 would move to about 1969. a6: 1990, Mentor Graphics' acquisition of Silicon Compiler Systems for about $110M -- a later, larger-scale event than the a5 crossing (techmonitor.ai).

name: Stephen Lake
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED TWICE OVER: ycombinator.com/companies/north names "Stephen Lake (Founder/CEO)" with the one-liner "Wearable computing hardware: biosignal gesture recognition" (founded 2012, batch Winter 2013, status Acquired), and North is entry 35 of the 91-company Y Combinator Top Companies list, verified by downloading https://yc-oss.github.io/api/companies/top.json with curl and indexing it rather than trusting the roster's claim. SERIAL-FOUNDER CHECK: no earlier venture. Lake, Matthew Bailey and Aaron Grant founded Thalmic Labs in 2012, the year all three took a BASc in mechatronics engineering at Waterloo; no source records any prior company or employer, and his other venture, Jetson, post-dates the 2020 acquisition. Thalmic Labs (renamed North in 2018) is both his first venture and the hit entity. acq50 FALLBACK USED -- FLAGGED, BECAUSE frame.md MAKES THE FALLBACK THE RARE EXCEPTION AND THIS ROW CLAIMS IT. a5 = 2020, Google's acquisition of North, reported by The Globe and Mail at approximately US$180M and relayed by BetaKit and silicon.co.uk; terms were never officially disclosed, so confidence is medium. The 2020 acq50 bar is $40,195,159 nominal, so $180M is 4.5x the bar -- no margin problem. NO CURRENCY CONVERSION NEEDED: BetaKit states the figure in US dollars. WHY THE FALLBACK IS NOT BARRED HERE, SET OUT IN FULL BECAUSE IT IS THE CONTESTABLE PART OF THIS ROW. frame.md bars the fallback whenever an earlier rev10 crossing is KNOWN, including on a purely qualitative claim that the venture was already large or profitable. No such claim exists for this company, and the sourced facts point the other way. What is sourced about scale is all funding and headcount, never revenue: about $200M raised in equity and debt by 2019, "one of the highest-funded pre-IPO companies in Canada" (TechCrunch, Aug 2019), 400-plus employees before roughly 150 were laid off in 2019, and ~200 at acquisition. What is sourced about commercial performance is uniformly bad: the Myo armband ($199.99, launched 1 May 2015) was discontinued in October 2018, Focals 1.0 shipped January 2019 and was discontinued that December, and Focals 2.0 never shipped at all. The only revenue-shaped numbers anywhere are from the February 2013 preorder campaign -- TechCrunch's "10,000 Pre-Orders In 2 Days, Which Adds Up To $1.5M In Sales", about $4M of preorders in the first month, and roughly 30,000 preorders reported later in 2013 -- all of which sit BELOW the 2013 rev10 bar of $7,235,970, and all of which are preorders for a device that did not ship until late 2014. Two further attempts (a WebSearch for Myo units sold and revenue for 2015-2016, and Brave-index queries for Focals unit sales) turned up no annual revenue figure for any year of this company's existence, from any source. Since no source establishes -- quantitatively or qualitatively -- that revenue ever reached the bar, the earlier crossing is not "known" and the fallback is permitted. An adversarial re-check should test exactly this: if a Myo or Focals unit-sales figure exists for any single year above roughly $7.4M, this row becomes a bounded rev10 instead. NOTE ON THE WEB SEARCH BUDGET: the session's shared 200-call WebSearch budget was exhausted partway through this person, so the last stage of research ran on WebFetch and curl against the Brave Search index only. a1: BOUNDED 1989-1990. Forbes' 30 Under 30 entry, published 18 January 2017, gives Lake's age as 27, which places his birth between January 1989 and January 1990. No source gives a birth date directly, so the bound rather than a point year is recorded. a2: 2012, BASc in mechatronics engineering, University of Waterloo -- high confidence, from the university's own engineering news page, which states that Lake, Bailey and Grant "all graduated with a BASc in Mechatronics in 2012", corroborated by uwaterloo.ca/alumni/news/interview-thalmic-labs describing them as "the three graduates of the UWaterloo Mechatronics Engineering Class of '12". This is a completed degree, not a dropout. a3: 2012, set equal to a4 under the R1 convention (the p26 Roddick / Sara Blakely precedent): the founding of Thalmic Labs is his first role in wearable-computing hardware, and no employer-paid job in the domain precedes it -- Waterloo's mechatronics programme is co-op, so he will have had student work terms, but no source names an employer or a year for any of them. Confidence low for that reason. a4: 2012, Thalmic Labs, founded in the same year the degree completed -- the near-zero education-to-venture gap the roster selected this row to test is real and confirmed. a6: unknown. The 2020 Google acquisition is already a5; nothing larger or later followed for this entity, which was absorbed and whose Focals support ended 31 July 2020.
